title: Dispensary Scams: How to Spot Fake Listings and Sellers
h1: How to Spot Fake Dispensary Listings and Online Weed Scams

body:
Dispensary scams usually start with a search result that looks right and end with money sent to a stranger. Fake search listings, copycat websites and sellers who promise to ship cannabis to your door are typical versions. The fix is simple: know the red flags, check the license and buy from a store you can walk into.

## How dispensary scams work: fake listings and copycat sites

Scammers borrow what makes a real store look trustworthy. They build websites that look official, or put their own phone number next to a real business's name in search results. Some promise home delivery, take payment through an app, then add fees and disappear. Any business with a public listing can be copied, so reach a store through its own website, not a link someone sends you.

## Red flags: shipping offers, payment-app requests and pressure to prepay

Walk away if a seller:

- Offers to ship or mail cannabis to your home, in any state
- Wants payment by Cash App, Venmo, Zelle, gift card, cryptocurrency or wire before you've seen a store
- Pushes you to pay now, or adds surprise fees for "insurance," "customs" or a "driver"
- Won't give a street address, or gives one that doesn't match the store's own website
- Never mentions checking your ID

The Federal Trade Commission warns that scammers like payment apps because it's hard to get your money back once you send it.

## Why licensed shops don't ship cannabis

As of October 2026, adult-use marijuana is still a Schedule I controlled substance under federal law. In 2021, the U.S. Postal Service said THC products other than hemp remain generally prohibited in the mail, even when the sender and buyer live in states that allow cannabis. Moving cannabis between states breaks federal law too.

So a "dispensary" offering to mail cannabis is either breaking federal law or planning to take your money and send nothing. Legal cannabis sales in Michigan go through licensed businesses, never the mail. Our guide to [cannabis delivery in Michigan](/blog/cannabis-delivery-michigan/) explains how that differs from a mail-order scam.

## How to check a Michigan retailer's state license

Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses adult-use and medical cannabis businesses. Its Verify a License tool has separate searches for adult-use establishments and medical facilities.

1. Search the business name or city in the agency's tool.
2. Make sure the licensed address matches the store you plan to visit.
3. Contact the store using details from its own website, not an ad or a text.
4. Expect an ID check at the counter. Michigan stores check ID before every sale, and legal products carry the state's required labels.

Our guide to [licensed vs. black market cannabis](/blog/licensed-vs-black-market-cannabis/) covers the other differences.

## Where to find High Society's real store pages, hours and online menu

High Society has eight Michigan stores: Big Rapids, Birch Run, Charlotte, East Lansing, Lenox, Mount Pleasant, New Buffalo and Saline. Each store page on our website lists its own address, hours and directions, so start from our [store locations](/dispensary-locations/) page rather than a search ad.

To order ahead, pick your store on our [online menu](/shop/), add items and choose a pickup time, in store or curbside. Bring a valid ID each time you pick up an order. Our guide to [ordering cannabis online](/blog/how-to-order-cannabis-online/) walks through each step, and our [FAQ](/faq/) covers common questions.

## If you already paid: bank, payment app, IC3 and FTC

Act fast:

1. **Call your bank or card issuer** and report the charge as fraud.
2. **Report it in the payment app.** The FTC notes that Cash App and Venmo take reports through in-app chat.
3. **File with IC3.** The FBI runs the Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov), the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime.
4. **Report to the FTC** at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
5. **Keep records:** screenshots, usernames, phone numbers, web addresses and receipts.

## Protecting personal data and security codes

- **Never share a one-time security code.** The FTC says anyone who asks for the code sent to your phone or email is a scammer.
- **Don't text photos of your ID** to an online seller. A licensed store checks ID in person.
- **Check the web address.** A copycat site may swap a letter or add a word to a real store's domain.

Adults 21 and older, and registered medical patients 18 and older, can shop legally at licensed Michigan stores. Valid ID required. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Can a dispensary ship weed to my house?
faq.a: No. Licensed Michigan dispensaries cannot mail cannabis. The Postal Service considers marijuana nonmailable, even between states where cannabis is legal, and moving cannabis between states breaks federal law. Any seller offering to ship cannabis to your home is a red flag, so buy in person or order ahead for pickup.

faq.q: Is it safe to pay for weed with Cash App or Venmo?
faq.a: Not when you're paying a seller you've never met. The FTC warns that scammers push payment apps because it's hard to get your money back. Licensed stores take payment at pickup or through their own checkout. At High Society, cash works, and other payment options vary by store.

faq.q: Where do I report a cannabis scam?
faq.a: Start with your bank or payment app to try to stop or reverse the payment. Then file reports with the FBI through ic3.gov and with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Save screenshots, usernames, phone numbers and receipts first, since they make your report more useful.

faq.q: How do I check if a Michigan dispensary is licensed?
faq.a: Use the Cannabis Regulatory Agency's online license search, which has separate lookups for adult-use establishments and medical facilities. Search the business name or city and compare the licensed address with the store you plan to visit. Licensed stores also check ID before every sale and sell products with Michigan's required labels.

sources.label: U.S. Postal Service: Treatment of E-Cigarettes in the Mail, final rule (Federal Register, Oct. 21, 2021), on THC-containing products being nonmailable, govinfo
Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Verify a License
Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Marihuana Rules, R 420.1 to R 420.1004 (ID check before each sale; labeling)
Federal Trade Commission: Mobile Payment Apps: How To Avoid a Scam When You Use One (May 2022)
Federal Trade Commission: What's a verification code and why would someone ask me for it? (consumer alert, March 7, 2024)

claims.claim: Takeaway and FAQ: "the Postal Service considers THC products nonmailable, even between legal states."
claims.fix: USPS makes an exception for hemp and hemp derivatives with no more than 0.3% THC, so "THC products" is too broad. Takeaway and FAQ now say "marijuana".
claims.evidence: "THC is generally nonmailable ... THC-containing substances remain generally prohibited under the CSA, regardless of whether ... the shipper or recipient resides in a State or locality that has decriminalized"; "The only exceptions to this mailing ban are for hemp and hemp derivatives that contain no more than 0.3 percent THC".

claims.claim: Body: "The U.S. Postal Service has said THC products remain generally prohibited in the mail, even when the sender and buyer live in states that allow cannabis."
claims.fix: The statement is from a 2021 rule (before the April 2026 federal rescheduling of state-medical marijuana) and excepts hemp. Reworded: "In 2021, the U.S. Postal Service said THC products other than hemp remain generally prohibited in the mail..."; sentence split.
claims.evidence: Rule effective October 21, 2021; quotes as above. Publication 52 sec. 453.31 (https://pe.usps.com/text/Pub52/pub52c4_020.htm): if distribution is unlawful under the CSA, "the mailing of the substance is also unlawful under 18 U.S.C. 1716".

claims.claim: Moving cannabis between states breaks federal law.
claims.evidence: "Taking cannabis across a state line ... remains illegal under federal law, even between two states where it is legal."

claims.claim: As of October 2026, adult-use marijuana is still a Schedule I controlled substance.
claims.evidence: "all other marijuana, including adult-use, is still Schedule I" (as of October 2026).

claims.claim: "Legal cannabis in Michigan moves through licensed businesses, never the mail."
claims.fix: Adults may also legally gift cannabis and grow at home, so not all legal cannabis moves through businesses. Reworded to "Legal cannabis sales in Michigan go through licensed businesses, never the mail."
claims.evidence: "Adults may give away up to 2.5 ounces ... to another adult 21+, as long as nothing is received in return"; "An adult may grow up to 12 plants for personal use at home".

claims.claim: Scam tactics: scammers copy a dispensary's name, logo and photos onto a lookalike site or social account, create a map listing with their own phone number, and post menus "with prices far below any licensed store" (intro also says "fake map listings").
claims.fix: Opened sources support lookalike official-looking websites, scammers' phone numbers placed next to a real business's name in search results, and fake dispensaries that promise delivery, take app payments, add fees and disappear; nothing opened supports the cut-price menus, the logo/photo/social detail or map listings specifically. Paragraph rewritten to the supported tactics; intro now says "fake search listings".
claims.evidence: FTC (Apr. 3, 2025): "They might even put their number alongside a trusted company's name"; "link to a website that looks official"; "Don't assume the phone number that comes up in search is legit." BBB via WWMT (https://www.wwmt.com/news/nation-world/marijuana-dispensary-scams-reportedly-on-the-rise-scammers-fake-website-customer-digital-wallet-better-business-bureau-dangercash-app-weed-pot-cannabis): "victims are attempting to purchase marijuana online with the promise of home delivery. But instead, scammers are creating fake websites and charging customers phony fees via cash apps"; NBC San Diego (June 28, 2023): "once they paid, the person they spoke with disappeared".

claims.claim: Red flags: payment by app, gift card, cryptocurrency or wire before seeing a store; surprise fees for "insurance"; no street address; no ID check.
claims.evidence: FTC (Aug. 5, 2020): "Never wire money, send gift cards, or give your account password in exchange for customer service help." BBB via NBC Connecticut (Jan. 24, 2023): fake dispensaries ask for payment "through a digital wallet app like Zelle or CashApp" and then another fee to "cover delivery insurance". ID check required before every sale (law-facts mi-au-purchase-limit).

claims.claim: The FTC warns that scammers like payment apps because it is hard to get your money back once you send it.
claims.evidence: "Some scammers may try to trick you into sending them money through a mobile payment app. That's because they know once you do, it's hard for you to get your money back." (May 2022)

claims.claim: Michigan's Cannabis Regulatory Agency licenses adult-use and medical cannabis businesses.
claims.evidence: "licenses and regulates adult-use and medical marijuana businesses".

claims.claim: The CRA's Verify a License tool has separate searches for adult-use establishments and medical facilities.
claims.evidence: Not re-opened (michigan.gov refuses automated fetches); confirmed through WebSearch 2026-10-24: the page "has separate lookups for adult-use establishments and medical marijuana facilities, plus tribal businesses and hemp processor-handler licenses". "Verify a License" is the tool's name, so the gate's meta-language review hit stands.

claims.claim: Michigan stores check ID before every sale, and legal products carry the state's required labels.
claims.evidence: "Before any sale the store must check a valid driver's license or government-issued photo ID showing the buyer is 21+"; R 420.504(1) label requirements.

claims.claim: High Society has eight Michigan stores: Big Rapids, Birch Run, Charlotte, East Lansing, Lenox, Mount Pleasant, New Buffalo and Saline; each store page lists its address, hours and directions.
claims.source: facts/hs-facts.json stores, conflicts "store count"; docs/BUILD-CONTRACT.md 3.1 store-details block
claims.evidence: Eight store slugs in hs-facts; "Say 8 stores; never '7'"; store-details renders address, phone, hours and a directions link on each store page. The article prints no phone, hours or address itself.

claims.claim: Order ahead on the online menu: pick a store, add items, choose a pickup time, in store or curbside.
claims.evidence: "Select your preferred products, choose the quantities, add them to your cart, and schedule a pick-up time"; "If curbside pickup is your preference, let us know"; "In-Store Pickup".

claims.claim: "First-time customers bring a valid ID."
claims.fix: Implies returning customers need no ID, but Michigan stores check ID before every sale. Reworded: "Bring a valid ID each time you pick up an order."
claims.evidence: "Before any sale the store must check a valid driver's license or government-issued photo ID". hs-facts services.ordering only says first-time online customers verify ID at checkout.

claims.claim: If you paid: call your bank or card issuer; report in the payment app (Cash App and Venmo take reports through in-app chat); report to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
claims.evidence: "Cash App recommends chatting through their app for the fastest service."; "Venmo recommends chatting through their app for the fastest service."; "report it to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov".

claims.claim: The FBI runs the Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov), the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime.
claims.evidence: "The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) is the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime. It is run by the FBI".

claims.claim: The FTC says anyone who asks for the code sent to your phone or email is a scammer.
claims.fix: Source replaced: the listed Military Consumer copy (a partner site) swapped for the FTC's own consumer alert, which carries the same post, so the attribution "The FTC says" matches its source.
claims.evidence: FTC consumer alert, March 7, 2024, Alvaro Puig: "Anyone who asks you for your account verification code is a scammer."

claims.claim: Don't text photos of your ID to an online seller; a licensed store checks ID in person.
claims.evidence: ID checked before the sale; "Bring a valid government-issued ID or passport and check in with our security and front desk upon arrival."

claims.claim: A copycat site may swap a letter or add a word to a real store's domain.
claims.evidence: FTC: scammers "link to a website that looks official". General advice, no figure.

claims.claim: Licensed stores take payment at pickup or through their own checkout; at High Society, cash works and other options vary by store.
claims.evidence: "a staff member will call your name, process your payment, and review the order"; "High Society accepts cash and debit cards."; credit conflicting, not stated.

claims.claim: Adults 21+, and registered medical patients 18+, can shop at licensed Michigan stores with a valid ID.
claims.evidence: "adults 21 and older may legally buy"; "Individuals 18 and older with a medical marijuana card can also make purchases."

review.notes: Writer's note kept: Michigan delivery licensing is left to the delivery article; copy does not imply High Society delivers. Fact-check 2026-10-24: 21 claims checked, 5 fixed (USPS 'THC products' narrowed to marijuana and dated to the 2021 rule; 'all legal cannabis moves through businesses' narrowed to sales; unsupported scam-tactic details replaced with FTC/BBB-supported ones; 'first-time customers bring ID' replaced with an every-pickup ID line), plus one source swapped to the FTC original. No phone numbers, hours or addresses printed. Sources: 6 (cap), all opened except the two michigan.gov entries (Verify a License confirmed through search; Marihuana Rules listed in law-facts).
